conflicts.point: Whether 'was there a signal for any inspector to catch' is a system-level fact resting on model weights plus the published tooling frontier, or whether reducibility-by-inspection is sector-relative all the way down like foreseeability.

positions.stance: Reducibility tracks the diligence a field can mount, so the supposedly system-independent fact collapses back into the domain-by-domain calibration it claimed to escape, making the detection gate a trigger litigated for a decade.

Signal extractability rides on the model weights plus the published interpretability tooling at a given time, which is identical across deployment sectors; sector-specific tooling is downstream interpretation, not the upstream existence of the extractable signal.

conflicts.point: Which trigger should fire the disclosure and liability obligation: an observable statutory decision class enforced by an existing regulator, or a pre-deployment gate keyed to demonstrated detection capacity for a class of emergent failure.

positions.stance: The legal line is the only boundary all parties can see before deployment and can be enforced near-term inside existing rulemaking; the detection gate waits on interpretability science only frontier-scale firms can prove they have.

The two triggers are complementary across a coverage boundary; the legal line fires nothing for a foundation model crossing into an un-homed decision class no agency names, which is exactly the emergent zone the detection gate is built to catch.

conflicts.point: Whether an independent standard-setting body can define and version a detection battery without capture, given that the firms with the deepest interpretability expertise are the ones being measured.

positions.stance: Only firms large enough to help write the harness can clear it, so a public commons launders the moat rather than removing it; demonstrating detection capacity may still require frontier-scale expertise, making the gate the deepest drawbridge.

Separating standard-setter from applicant—the aviation/NTSB and FDA endpoint model—dissolves the moat because clearing the gate means passing a public test rather than building proprietary science, provided the standard-setter is not the body being measured.

conflicts.point: Whether existing sector regulators hold statutory authority to mandate court-admissible model logging through current rulemaking, or whether fresh legislation is required.

positions.stance: The ECOA enforcer, EEOC, and FDA already hold jurisdiction over credit, employment, and diagnostic decisions and can extend a logging mandate inside rulemaking they already run, near-term and with no new science.

That the agencies can add a court-admissible logging mandate without new legislation is an unverified legal assertion; if fresh authorization is needed, the near-term advantage collapses and coverage becomes the only thing separating the two triggers.

verdicts.conflict: Whether signal reducibility-by-inspection is a system-level fact resting on model weights plus published tooling, or sector-relative all the way down like foreseeability.
verdicts.rationale: C22 draws a coherent distinction between the upstream existence of an extractable signal in fixed model weights and the downstream act of interpreting it, which the same foundation model carries identically into any sector. C21 conflates the diligence a field can mount with the existence of the signal, and so does not rebut the claim that internals are constant across deployment contexts. C21's stronger move would require showing that the signal itself, not just the interpretive capacity, varies by sector, which it does not establish.
verdicts.whatWouldChange: Empirical demonstration that identical model weights yield genuinely different extractable signals depending on deployment sector, rather than merely different interpretive resources applied to the same signal, would flip the verdict toward C21.

verdicts.conflict: Which trigger should fire disclosure and liability: an observable statutory decision class enforced by an existing regulator, or a pre-deployment gate keyed to demonstrated detection capacity for emergent failure.
verdicts.rationale: C19 identifies a concrete coverage gap the statutory-line trigger leaves open: a foundation model crossing into a decision class no agency names fires no obligation under the legal-line approach. C16 offers a more administrable near-term mechanism but does not answer the un-homed-emergent-zone case. C19 frames the two triggers as complementary rather than rival, which accounts for more of the relevant deployment space, though it concedes the legal line works where a decision class is already named.
verdicts.whatWouldChange: Evidence that emergent harms in practice almost always land within an existing named decision class, leaving the un-homed zone empty, would reduce C19's scope advantage and favor the simpler single trigger in C16.

verdicts.conflict: Whether an independent standard-setting body can define a detection battery without capture, given that the firms with the deepest interpretability expertise are the ones being measured.
verdicts.rationale: C23 cites the FDA-endpoint and NTSB models as precedents for separating standard-setter from applicant, which supplies an authority-grounded mechanism. C25 raises an unrebutted structural objection: if only frontier-scale firms can staff the expertise to clear or co-author the harness, separation of roles does not remove the underlying capability moat. Neither side supplies direct evidence on whether a publicly funded evaluation commons (C28) can actually generate detection capacity independent of the measured firms, which is the load-bearing empirical question.
verdicts.whatWouldChange: Data on whether public bodies like NTSB or FDA developed evaluative capacity independent of the regulated industry, or whether a funded interpretability commons can match frontier-lab tooling, would resolve this; a demonstrated capture-resistant commons favors C23, persistent dependence on measured firms favors C25.

verdicts.conflict: Whether existing sector regulators hold statutory authority to mandate court-admissible model logging through current rulemaking, or whether fresh legislation is required.
verdicts.rationale: C24 names specific jurisdictional anchors (ECOA, EEOC, FDA) over credit, employment, and diagnostic decisions, which is concrete and testable. C26 correctly flags that the leap from existing jurisdiction to a court-admissible logging mandate without new authorization is an asserted but unverified legal proposition. The disagreement turns on an unresolved statutory-interpretation question that neither side settles with citation to specific rulemaking authority or case law.
verdicts.whatWouldChange: A legal analysis or agency action showing whether ECOA, Title VII, or FDA authorities encompass mandatory court-admissible model logging without new legislation would resolve this directly; confirmed existing authority favors C24, a need for fresh authorization favors C26 and collapses the speed advantage.

verdicts.conflict: Whether tiering compliance burden by firm size answers the entrenchment objection, or whether the substantive evaluation burden itself entrenches incumbents.
verdicts.rationale: C28 identifies that the binding constraint is the substantive evaluation burden, not the paperwork, so tiering documentation alone (C27) leaves the entrenching cost untouched, as the C28 critique of C27 establishes. C28 proposes socializing the evaluation science through a publicly funded commons, modeled on FDA clinical-trial infrastructure, which directly targets the identified constraint. The proposal's effectiveness remains contingent on the unresolved commons-capacity question shared with the C23/C25 conflict.
verdicts.whatWouldChange: Evidence that the substantive evaluation burden is in fact dominated by documentation cost rather than expertise cost would restore C27; evidence that a funded commons cannot supply frontier-grade evaluation capacity would undercut C28's proposed remedy.

verdicts.conflict: Whether liability priced off courtroom harm leaves most AI harm undeterred because victims cannot identify AI-shaped decisions, and whether this argues for abandonment or supplementation.
verdicts.rationale: C1 establishes a real detection gap supported by survey evidence (C2), but the inference that liability fails as a deterrent does not follow, because liability shapes pre-harm design choices independent of whether any victim sues. C5 accepts the empirical gap and redirects it toward supplementation with forward-looking deployment gates rather than abandonment, which preserves C1's evidence while closing its logical overreach. C5 does not dispute the data, only the conclusion drawn from it.
verdicts.whatWouldChange: Evidence that developers do not in fact adjust design choices in anticipation of liability absent litigation pressure would strengthen C1's abandonment inference against C5.

verdicts.conflict: Whether severed causation in the multi-tiered AI lifecycle defeats both liability regimes, or whether joint-and-several upstream liability resolves it without tracing a clean chain.
verdicts.rationale: C3 assumes liability requires a traceable single failure mode, importing component-part doctrine's clean-chain premise. C12 shows that joint-and-several upstream liability is designed precisely to assign cost without identifying one cause, so the severed-chain problem does not defeat the regime, and design-defect doctrine has attached to manufacturers regardless of operator behavior since the 1960s. The precedent C12 invokes directly addresses the causation premise C3 relies on.
verdicts.whatWouldChange: Doctrinal evidence that joint-and-several or design-defect liability cannot survive when runtime fine-tuning materially diverges from the shipped artifact would favor C3.

verdicts.conflict: Whether foreseeability-availability is a genuine cross-domain criterion for strict liability, or collapses into per-domain calibration because foreseeability is a sector-constructed threshold.
verdicts.rationale: C9 asserts a single cross-domain line where foreseeability is structurally unavailable, but C10 shows the same opaque output counts as foreseeable in medicine and invisible in credit because each sector's standard of care constructs the threshold. This means the proposed criterion still requires per-domain determination at the point of application, undercutting its claim to escape calibration. C9's supporting ultrahazardous analogy (C11) is separately weakened by C13's point that ultrahazardous status attaches to named bounded hazards, not unnamed emergent behavior.
verdicts.whatWouldChange: A demonstration that foreseeability-availability can be assessed at the model level prior to and independent of any sector's standard of care, as C22 attempts for signal extractability, would rehabilitate C9 as genuinely cross-domain.
